state.misconception_label: Divides total amount by each side of the ratio instead of dividing by the sum of the parts

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: In the diagram, AN : NB \( =3: 5 \) What is the distance AN? ![A line that begins with point A, ends with point B, and has point N in between. The entire length of the line measures 48 m.](). I got \( 16 \mathrm{~m} \) because I added the parts of the ratio as if they were a total.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Great job trying to apply the ratio, but remember that when finding the distance of AN, you need to divide the total length by the sum of the parts in the ratio. Try dividing 48 m by the sum of 3 and 5 to find the correct distance of AN. Keep up the good work!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so I need to add 3 and 5 together first to get 8, and then divide 48 by 8? That gives me 6, so would AN be 3 times 6 which is 18 m?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's correct! You've got the right idea now. Since the sum of the parts is 8, dividing 48 by 8 gives you 6. And multiplying 3 by 6 does indeed give you the correct distance of AN as 18 m. Keep up the good work with applying ratios in this way!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Yeah, that makes sense now! So basically I need to add up all the parts of the ratio first to get the total number of parts, and then divide the actual distance by that to find what one part is worth. Would this work the same way if the ratio was something like 2:3:5 instead, or does it get more complicated?
